blocks.text: Start With One Useful Page

Notion can build huge systems, but your first win is smaller: one page that catches loose thoughts before they disappear. You will build Quick Capture, then learn only the controls needed to keep it useful.
Pages Hold Your Work
A Notion page is a flexible space for text, tasks, images, links, and even other pages. Think of it as a document that can grow with your work instead of a blank canvas you must perfect.
Blocks Are the Building Pieces
Every paragraph, heading, checklist item, and callout is a block. Click a block to edit it. Use the six-dot handle beside it to move, duplicate, transform, or delete it.

blocks.question: You want to move one checklist item above another. What should you use?

feedbackCorrect.text: The handle controls one block without changing the rest of the page.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Meet the Slash Command
Type / on an empty line to open the block menu. Continue typing a block name, such as /todo or /callout, to reach it faster.
Give Information a Job
Use a heading to label a section, a to-do for an action, and a callout for something worth noticing. Plain text is best for everything that does not need special treatment.
Transform Instead of Retyping
Made a paragraph that should be a task? Open its block menu and choose Turn into. The words stay in place while the block changes its job.

blocks.title: Build a Clean Section
blocks.prompt: Put these actions in the simplest order.

feedbackCorrect.text: That sequence keeps each step clear and lightweight.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Start with the source or capture step, then organize only what is needed.

blocks.text: Create a Tiny Capture Structure
Your Quick Capture page needs only three sections: Tasks, Notes, and Links. This is temporary storage, not a forever filing system.

blocks.title: Keep It Frictionless
blocks.text: If capturing an idea requires choosing five tags, you will stop capturing. Write first. Organize during your weekly reset.
Fix Mistakes Fast
Use Cmd/Ctrl + Z when a block moves or changes unexpectedly. For a block you no longer need, open its handle menu and choose Delete.

blocks.title: Choose the Right Block
blocks.prompt: Match each need with the simplest block.

blocks.text: Formatting Is a Signal
Bold one phrase that matters. Highlight only true warnings. Too many colors and styles make everything compete, so nothing feels important.
Name It for the Moment of Use
Call the page Quick Capture, not Ideas 2026 Final or Personal Knowledge Inbox. A clear name helps you find it when you are rushed.

blocks.title: Build Your Quick Capture Page
blocks.prompt: Create a page named Quick Capture. Add Tasks, Notes, and Links headings, one to-do, one note, and one useful link.

blocks.question: A Quick Capture page should fully organize every item the moment you add it.

feedbackCorrect.text: Capture should be fast. Organizing belongs in a later review.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Recheck the lesson rule, then try again.

blocks.text: Your First Visible Win
You now have one trusted place for anything that arrives during the day. Tomorrow, open this page before creating another place to store the same kind of information.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
blocks.text: Build with blocks, use the slash command, and keep capture simple. A useful page beats a beautiful system you avoid.

lessons.title: Turn Chaos Into a Simple Home

blocks.text: A Home, Not a Maze
Your workspace needs a front door. My Life Hub will point to the few places you use often, without hiding them inside a deep folder tree.
The Sidebar Is Navigation
The sidebar shows pages you can open quickly. It is not a challenge to fill every level. Keep active pages easy to reach and let search handle the rest.
Create the Hub
Make a new page named My Life Hub. Add three headings: Work, Life, and Notes. These are signposts, not new databases.

blocks.question: Where should your most-used dashboard live?

options.label: Near the top level of your sidebar

feedbackCorrect.text: Frequent destinations should take as few clicks as possible.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Nest Pages With Purpose
A page can live inside another page. Nest reference material when the parent gives it useful context, such as Onboarding Notes inside Work.
Avoid Folder Thinking
Notion pages can link to one another and appear in databases. You do not need a perfect folder for every item before you can move forward.
Link Instead of Duplicate
Type @ followed by a page name, or use Link to page, to create a shortcut. One source page can appear in several useful places without being copied.

blocks.title: Nest or Link?
blocks.prompt: Choose the lighter action.

blocks.text: Favorite the Front Door
Add My Life Hub and Quick Capture to Favorites. Favorites are for a small working set, not every page you have ever created.

blocks.title: The Five-Item Rule
blocks.text: Keep five or fewer pages in Favorites. When everything is favorite, the list stops helping.
Search Beats Scrolling
Use Search when you remember a page title or phrase. Search is faster than opening several nested pages and guessing where something lives.

blocks.question: You need Quick Capture under both Work and Life. What is simplest?

options.label: Link to the same page from both sections
Move it back and forth each day

feedbackCorrect.text: Links keep one source of truth while improving access.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Use Clear Names
Choose names based on what you expect to find: Client Onboarding, Job Search, or Home Admin. Labels such as Stuff and Misc force your future self to open every page.
Leave Breathing Room
A divider or blank space can separate sections, but decoration should not push useful links below the fold. Your dashboard is a control panel, not a mood board.

screens.title: Build the My Life Hub Shell

blocks.title: Build the My Life Hub Shell
blocks.prompt: Create Work, Life, and Notes sections. Link Quick Capture, add one useful page under each section, then favorite the hub.

blocks.question: Duplicating a page is the best way to make it accessible from two sections.

feedbackCorrect.text: Link to one source page so updates never split across copies.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Recheck the lesson rule, then try again.

blocks.text: Test the Front Door
Close the page, return to the sidebar, and reopen My Life Hub. Make sure Quick Capture and your three sections are visible without hunting.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
blocks.text: Keep the hub shallow, link to existing pages, and use Favorites only for frequent destinations.

blocks.text: One List for Every Commitment
Work tasks, errands, and side projects can share one database. A property tells you what each item means, so you do not need a separate list for every part of life.
A Database Is a Collection of Pages
Every row in a Notion database is also a page. The row shows structured details; opening it gives you space for notes, links, and context.
Create Tasks
Inside My Life Hub, create a full-page database named Tasks. Keep the default title property and rename it Task.

blocks.question: What is each row inside a Notion database?

feedbackCorrect.text: Database items stay flexible because every row opens as a page.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Property 1: Status
Add a Status property with To-do, In progress, and Done. Status answers one question: where is this task now?
Property 2: Priority
Add a Select property called Priority with High, Medium, and Low. Use High only when delay has a real consequence.
Property 3: Due Date
Add a Date property called Due. Dates are for genuine deadlines or planned work, not a promise that everything is urgent.

blocks.title: Pick the Property
blocks.prompt: Match the information to its property.

blocks.text: Start With Real Tasks
Add five current commitments: one work deadline, one meeting follow-up, one job or career action, one life admin item, and one side-project step.

blocks.title: Do Not Add More Fields Yet
blocks.text: Owner, effort, category, energy, and formulas sound useful. Add a property only after you repeatedly need a decision it can support.
Open a Task Page
Open your meeting follow-up task. Add the context, the expected result, and any useful link inside the page body. Keep properties for facts you need to filter.

blocks.question: Where should a long meeting brief live?

feedbackCorrect.text: The page body holds context; properties keep the list scannable.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Write Action Titles
Begin task names with a verb: Send recap, Review deck, Book dentist. A noun such as Presentation describes a topic but does not tell you what done means.
Define Done
Before saving an important task, ask what visible result proves completion. Submit revised deck is clearer than Work on deck.

blocks.title: Add Five Real Tasks
blocks.prompt: Create five verb-led tasks. Give each a Status, Priority, and Due date, then add context inside at least one task page.

blocks.title: Capture a New Commitment
blocks.prompt: Use this order when a request arrives.
items: Add context inside the task page
correctItems: Add context inside the task page

feedbackCorrect.text: That sequence keeps each step clear and lightweight.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Start with the source or capture step, then organize only what is needed.

blocks.text: One Database, Less Maintenance
You now have one trusted Tasks database. Different views will show work and life separately later, without creating duplicate storage.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
blocks.text: Every task is a page. Use only Task, Status, Priority, and Due until real usage proves you need more.

blocks.text: Same Tasks, Different Lenses
A view changes how one database appears. Your tasks stay in one place while a table, board, or calendar answers a different question.
Start With Table
Table is best for scanning properties and cleaning data. Keep it as your All Tasks view so you always have one unfiltered place to check.
Add a Board
Create a Board view grouped by Status. Move a card between columns to update its status while keeping the same underlying task page.

blocks.question: Moving a task card from To-do to Done changes what?

feedbackCorrect.text: A board visualizes and edits the same database properties.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Add a Calendar
Create a Calendar view using Due. Tasks without a due date will not appear on the calendar, but they remain safely stored in Tasks.
Views Do Not Duplicate Data
Edit a task title in Calendar and the change appears in Table and Board. There is still only one task page.
Filter for Today
Duplicate your table view, name it Today, and filter Due to today. Add a second filter that hides tasks with Status Done.

blocks.title: Create a Useful View
blocks.prompt: Put the setup steps in order.

feedbackCorrect.text: That sequence keeps each step clear and lightweight.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Start with the source or capture step, then organize only what is needed.

blocks.text: Filter for This Week
Create This Week and show unfinished tasks due within the current week. This view turns a long list into a short planning surface.

blocks.title: Empty Can Be Good
blocks.text: An empty Today view means nothing is due today. Do not invent busywork just to make the dashboard look active.
Create a Done View
Add a List view named Done filtered to Status Done. Sort by Due descending so recent wins appear first.

blocks.title: Choose the View
blocks.prompt: Match each question to a view.

blocks.text: Hide Visual Noise
Each view can hide properties it does not need. Today may show Priority and Due, while Calendar may hide Status to keep each card short.
Sort for Decisions
In Today, sort High priority first and then earliest Due. Sorting should help you choose the next action, not simply make the table look tidy.

blocks.title: Create Three Working Views
blocks.prompt: Build Today, This Week, and Done from the same Tasks database. Confirm that editing one task updates every view.

blocks.question: A new database view creates a separate copy of every task.

feedbackCorrect.text: Views are different presentations of one shared set of task pages.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Recheck the lesson rule, then try again.

blocks.text: Run the Thirty-Second Test
Open Tasks and find today's work, this week's deadlines, and your latest completed task. If any answer takes longer than thirty seconds, simplify the filters or labels.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
blocks.text: Store tasks once. Use views, filters, and sorting to reveal the right work at the right moment.

units.title: Make Notion Work for Your Life

blocks.text: Notes Need a Return Path
A note is useful only if you can find and act on it later. You will create one Notes database and one repeatable meeting template.
Create Notes
Create a database named Notes. Keep the title property, then add a Date property and a Type select with Meeting, Reference, and Idea.
Every Note Is a Page
The database row keeps the title, date, and type visible. Open the row to write the full note, add links, or mention related pages.

blocks.question: Where should the full meeting discussion live?

feedbackCorrect.text: Properties help retrieval; the page body holds the actual note.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Use a Repeatable Shape
Create three headings inside a meeting note: Context, Key Points, and Next Actions. This makes scanning easier before the next meeting.
Context Explains Why
Write one or two lines on the meeting goal, attendees, and decision needed. Do not transcribe the calendar invitation.
Key Points Capture Meaning
Record decisions, constraints, and useful evidence. Skip sentences that merely repeat what everyone already knew.

blocks.title: Place the Note
blocks.prompt: Match each detail to its section.

blocks.text: Next Actions Need Owners
Write each action with a verb, owner, and date when known. If the action belongs to you, also add it to Tasks after the meeting.

blocks.title: Notes Are Not Tasks
blocks.text: Notes preserve context. Tasks drive action. Do not rely on a bullet buried inside meeting notes for something you must deliver.
Save It as a Template
Open the database template menu, create a new template, and add the three headings. New meeting notes can now start ready instead of blank.

blocks.question: A follow-up belongs to you and has a Friday deadline. Where should it go?

options.label: In Next Actions and the Tasks database

feedbackCorrect.text: Keep the context in Notes and the commitment in Tasks.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Name Notes for Retrieval
Use names such as Weekly Sync — Aug 4 or Client Launch Decision. Avoid Meeting Notes, because the title will become meaningless after several weeks.
Keep the Database Small
Do not create separate databases for meetings, ideas, and references. The Type property already separates them when a view needs to.

blocks.title: Create Your Meeting Template
blocks.prompt: Build Notes with Date and Type. Save a template containing Context, Key Points, and Next Actions, then create one sample meeting note.

blocks.question: Every kind of note needs its own database.

feedbackCorrect.text: One Notes database plus a Type property is simpler to maintain and search.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Recheck the lesson rule, then try again.

blocks.text: Test Future You
Search for the sample note, open it, and identify the decision and next action in under thirty seconds. Rename or simplify sections if you cannot.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
blocks.text: Store notes once, use a predictable template, and move personal commitments into Tasks.

blocks.text: Turn the Hub Into a Daily Tool
Your My Life Hub already has navigation. Now it will show the small set of tasks and notes you need without opening full databases.
Linked Views Reuse the Source
A linked view displays an existing database somewhere else. It does not copy the data, so edits still update the original Tasks or Notes database.
Add Today to the Hub
Under Work, insert a linked view of Tasks. Select the Today view or recreate its filters, then hide every property except Status, Priority, and Due.

blocks.question: What happens when you complete a task in a linked Today view?

feedbackCorrect.text: Linked views edit the same source database.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Add This Week
Place a linked This Week view below Today. Keep it collapsed or lower on the page so urgent work stays visible first.
Add Recent Notes
Under Notes, link the Notes database. Sort Date newest first and limit your attention to recent meeting and reference notes.

blocks.text: Share the Result, Not Your Whole Life
Your hub mixes work and private information. Collaboration starts by choosing the smallest page another person actually needs.
Private Is the Safe Default
Keep My Life Hub, Tasks, and Notes private unless collaboration requires access. Share a specific meeting note instead of the entire system.
Open the Share Menu
On the meeting note, select Share, invite the intended person, and review the permission before sending. Page access can also affect content nested underneath it.

blocks.question: A teammate needs to read one meeting recap. What should you share?

feedbackCorrect.text: The narrowest useful access reduces accidental exposure.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Choose the Smallest Permission
Use view access for reading, comment access for feedback, and edit access only when the person must change the content.
Guests Are Page-Specific
A guest can be invited to selected pages without becoming a full workspace member. This works well for a client, mentor, or external collaborator.
Comments Keep Feedback Attached
Select text or use the comment control to ask a focused question. The discussion stays beside the work instead of getting lost in another chat thread.

blocks.title: Choose the Permission
blocks.prompt: Match the need to the lightest permission.

blocks.text: Mention With Intention
Use @name when a specific person needs the update. Avoid mentioning everyone for information that does not require attention.

blocks.title: Check the Parent Page
blocks.text: Before sharing a page, confirm where it lives. Access inherited through a parent can be broader than the invitation you are about to send.
Public Links Need Extra Care
Publishing to the web is different from inviting a known person. Do not publish private notes, personal details, internal links, or confidential work.

blocks.question: A client needs to suggest wording but should not rewrite the page. Which access fits?

feedbackCorrect.text: Comment access supports feedback without allowing direct changes.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Review Before You Send
Scan the page body, properties, backlinks, and nested pages. Remove private context that the recipient does not need.
Test From Their Point of View
Confirm the recipient can open the intended page and cannot navigate into My Life Hub. If possible, use the permission preview or a separate browser session.

blocks.title: Share One Meeting Note Safely
blocks.prompt: Choose a sample note, remove private details, invite a trusted person with view or comment access, and verify My Life Hub remains private.

blocks.question: Sharing My Life Hub is necessary when someone only needs one meeting note.

feedbackCorrect.text: Share the smallest useful page and keep the dashboard private.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Recheck the lesson rule, then try again.

blocks.text: Revoke Access When It Ends
Return to Share after the review or project finishes. Remove guests and public links that no longer have a reason to exist.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
blocks.text: Share the smallest useful page, grant the lightest permission, and verify access from the recipient's point of view.

Make the Whole System Work
You have built every piece. This final lesson connects capture, action, notes, review, and mobile use into one calm workflow.
Your System Has Four Doors
My Life Hub is the home. Quick Capture catches interruptions. Tasks holds commitments. Notes holds reusable context. Everything else is optional.
Check the Top of the Hub
The first screen should show Quick Capture, Today, and your most useful recent notes. Move anything less important lower.

blocks.question: Which item deserves the highest position on a daily dashboard?

feedbackCorrect.text: Daily decisions should appear before decoration and history.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Remove Duplicate Storage
Search for extra task lists or note databases created during practice. Move useful items into Tasks or Notes, then archive the empty duplicates.
Hide Unused Properties
If a property has not helped you decide, filter, or sort anything, hide or remove it. Simpler databases are faster to maintain.
Keep the Visual System Quiet
Use one accent color, clear headings, and limited callouts. Widgets and covers are optional; fast navigation is not.

blocks.title: From Request to Archive
blocks.prompt: Put the complete workflow in order.
items: Turn it into a clear task
correctItems: Turn it into a clear task

feedbackCorrect.text: That sequence keeps each step clear and lightweight.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Start with the source or capture step, then organize only what is needed.

blocks.text: Set Up Mobile Capture
Open Notion on your phone, find Quick Capture, and add it to Favorites. Mobile is for fast entry, not rebuilding database settings.

blocks.title: Use Desktop for Structure
blocks.text: Create views, templates, and permissions on desktop or web. Use mobile to capture, check Today, and mark simple tasks done.
Run a Real Scenario
Imagine your manager asks for a Friday launch update. Capture the request, create a dated task, and open the task page for context.

blocks.title: Complete the Workflow
blocks.prompt: Match each piece of the launch request to its home.

blocks.text: Finish and Preserve Context
Mark the task Done after sending the update. Save only the decisions or reference material you may need again inside Notes.
Run the Thirty-Second Test
From My Life Hub, find today's tasks, your latest note, and Quick Capture. Complete all three checks in under thirty seconds.

blocks.title: Complete the Final Challenge
blocks.prompt: Process one real request from capture to completion. Then run the thirty-second test on desktop and add one item from mobile.

blocks.question: A finished Life Hub should keep growing new databases for every project.

feedbackCorrect.text: Reuse Tasks and Notes until a real limitation proves another database is necessary.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Recheck the lesson rule, then try again.

blocks.text: Your Maintenance Rule
Use the system for one week before redesigning it. During the weekly reset, fix only the friction you actually experienced.

blocks.title: Course Complete
blocks.text: You built a simple My Life Hub with one Tasks database, one Notes database, fast capture, focused views, and safe sharing.

lessons.title: Let Notion AI Help, Not Take Over

blocks.text: Optional Means Optional
Your My Life Hub already works without AI. Continue only if Notion AI is available in your plan or trial; no core workflow depends on it.
Use AI for Transformation
AI is most useful when you already have source material. Ask it to summarize, restructure, or extract actions instead of inventing facts from nothing.
Start With a Messy Note
Open a non-sensitive sample note containing several ideas. Ask Notion AI to summarize the decisions in three bullets without adding new information.

blocks.question: Which request gives AI the safest job?

options.label: Summarize these notes without adding facts
Guess what the client secretly wants

feedbackCorrect.text: A bounded transformation is easier to verify than invented context.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Extract Action Items
Ask AI to list actions with an owner and due date only when those details appear in the note. Missing information should be marked as unknown.
Compare With the Source
Read every generated action against the original note. Remove invented owners, dates, or commitments before moving anything into Tasks.
Ask Your Workspace
When workspace search is available, ask a specific question such as: What launch date was agreed in the latest project note? Open the cited page before relying on the answer.

blocks.title: Use AI Responsibly
blocks.prompt: Put the workflow in order.
items: Compare the output with the source
correctItems: Compare the output with the source

feedbackCorrect.text: That sequence keeps each step clear and lightweight.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Start with the source or capture step, then organize only what is needed.

blocks.text: Protect Sensitive Information
Do not paste passwords, private identity details, confidential client data, or information you are not allowed to process. Follow your employer's AI policy.

blocks.title: Availability Can Change
blocks.text: AI features, limits, and plan access may change. Treat the feature as an accelerator, never as a requirement for using your hub.
A Better Summary Request
State the source, output shape, limit, and guardrail: Summarize this meeting in three bullets. Include decisions only. Mark unclear points instead of guessing.

blocks.question: AI assigns Friday as a due date, but the source note has no date. What should you do?

options.label: Remove it or mark the date unknown

feedbackCorrect.text: Generated details must be supported by the source.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Look for the choice that keeps the system simple and preserves one source of truth.

blocks.text: Keep Human Decisions Human
AI can suggest structure, but you decide priority, permission, and whether a commitment belongs in Tasks. Those choices depend on consequences the tool may not know.
Save the Useful Result
After checking the summary, keep it in the note page. Move only verified commitments into Tasks, using the same four properties from the core course.

blocks.title: Run One Checked AI Assist
blocks.prompt: Use a non-sensitive sample note. Generate a three-bullet summary and action list, compare both with the source, and correct every unsupported detail.

blocks.question: If AI produces a confident answer, checking the source is unnecessary.

feedbackCorrect.text: Confidence is not evidence. Verify names, dates, decisions, and commitments.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Recheck the lesson rule, then try again.

blocks.text: Know When to Skip AI
For a two-line note or one obvious task, manual editing is faster. Use AI only when the time saved is greater than the time needed to check it.

blocks.title: Bonus Takeaway
blocks.text: Give AI bounded transformation jobs, protect sensitive data, verify against the source, and keep the core system usable without it.
